content: The program is supported by a network of peer educators who are trained in participatory community mobilization and empowerment. It provides HIV testing and counseling (HTC), syndromic treatment for sexually transmitted infections (STIs), contraceptives, health education, and legal advice. Cervical screening is being implemented, with nurses trained in visual inspection and cryotherapy for the treatment of precancerous lesions. Peer educators conduct community mobilization sessions addressing issues relevant to sex workers, such as self-worth, behavior change, contraception, HIV, and cervical cancer. They also address topics related to clients and partners, including communication, assertiveness, serodiscordance, sexual networks, and concurrent partnerships. Additionally, they focus on issues within the sisterhood, such as advocacy, stigma, rights, and support. Since 2009, the program has expanded from five sites to a national network of 36 sites, including six fixed facilities and 30 outreach sites. By 2013, it had served over 14,000 women. At one site where population-based surveys were conducted, the proportion of HIV-negative women who reported recent HIV testing increased from 35% in 2011 to over 70% in 2013. During the same period, the proportion of women living with HIV who were receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART) rose from 28% to 45%. COTRAVEDT provides human rights-based training for peer educators who work with sex workers, gay and transgender individuals, and men who have sex with men. These peer educators offer information, support, and referrals to address the sexual health needs of the community. They also foster solidarity and trust among transgender sex workers through support groups that connect younger transgender women with older, more experienced ones. This approach emphasizes the importance of sexual expression, self-determination, autonomy, and fairness. Peer educators are trained to understand the complexities of individuals' lives, including the psychosocial and structural risks of HIV, and to deliver outreach that goes beyond negative, disease-focused messaging. COTRAVEDT interventions have significantly enhanced the capacity of peer educators and volunteers to meet the needs of transgender and transvestite sex workers by providing appropriate services and referrals. The organization has also participated in national consultations on sex work and has worked to break down barriers of discrimination and misunderstanding through media outreach, including 12 radio and television interviews. With nearly 1,300 sex workers reached through peer education, there has been a reported increase in solidarity among sex workers and greater utilization of mobile clinic services, demonstrating the effectiveness of COTRAVEDT's approaches. Faced with the lack of a comprehensive health policy addressing the specific needs of the transgender population and a shortage of experienced healthcare providers, the Silueta X Association launched a program to promote health among young transgender individuals and prevent the risks associated with non-professional feminizing hormone regimens. A participatory process was used to design a project that met the demand for information on gender transition. Due to the unavailability of public-sector doctors and nurses for workshops at times convenient for the transgender community, the project enlisted a private-sector doctor and an Ecuadorian endocrinology specialist based in Chile to train activists and the target group. Approximately 160 young transgender individuals aged 15–29 directly benefited from the program. Peer communication was the primary strategy for spreading awareness about the program, using social networks and other virtual communication channels. This approach helped identify a new generation of potential users of feminizing hormone regimens. However, education on the risks of feminizing hormone regimens remains necessary, including collaboration with other transgender organizations in Ecuador. After project funding ended, Silueta X continued to incorporate information on proper feminizing hormone regimens into its training for those involved in HIV prevention, as well as in recreational and social events like beauty pageants. The Health Outreach to Teens (HOTT) program in New York City serves LGBTQ adolescents, homeless or unstably housed youth, and those living with HIV through an on-site medical suite and a mobile medical unit. HOTT provides acute and primary care, mental health services, HIV testing, case management, and health education. In 2013, approximately 11% of the 1,100 young people receiving services identified as transgender, many of whom were people of color, homeless, or at risk of homelessness, and facing other psychosocial stressors. To engage and support these youth, the program offers a trans-affirming environment, free care, and rapid access to appointments. HOTT staff monitor risks and resilience factors and connect clients to preventive services emphasizing harm reduction. To ensure a trans-affirming environment, all HOTT staff, including medical providers, nurses, case managers, and HIV test providers—many of whom identify as members of the LGBTQ community—are trained in transgender-competent service provision. Trans-inclusive program literature and health education materials are available. HOTT’s weekly transgender women’s support group, The Girls Room, successfully engages this hard-to-reach population and provides a safe space for exploring and supporting gender transition. A Youth Advisory Board and The Girls Room provide feedback on transgender services, and annual clinic-wide surveys evaluate service effectiveness. The Center of Excellence for Transgender Health aims to increase access to comprehensive, effective, and affirming healthcare services for transgender and gender-variant communities. Its ultimate goal is to improve the overall health and well-being of transgender individuals by developing and implementing programs that address community-identified needs. The Center’s projects address a wide range of health issues for transgender people, including primary and preventive care, hormone therapy, mental health, youth services, and surgical care. The Transitions Project builds the capacity of community-based organizations to adapt, implement, and evaluate evidence-based HIV prevention interventions for transgender communities. The Transgender Family Program, established in 2004 at the Community Healthcare Network clinics in New York City, aims to improve access to HIV prevention and primary healthcare services. The program integrates comprehensive transgender services into community health clinics through community mapping, consultations, forums, and reviews of similar programs. Patients were invited to form a Client Advisory Board to guide the integration and implementation of services for the transgender community. Integrated services include transgender care, HIV testing and counseling, medical case management, treatment adherence support, STI screening and treatment, prevention interventions, and mental health and nutritional services. The program also provides risk reduction counseling, support groups, outreach, bilingual educational workshops, and referrals to legal and social services. Recruitment strategies for staff members and trained peer leaders include face-to-face contact, community-based activities, and online methods such as advertising and social media tools. Clients are encouraged to involve family members, which has proven to be an effective strategy for increasing access and attendance. Over 750 people have received transgender-specific services. Identified benefits of integrated transgender services include improved community tolerance and acceptance, increased accessibility through convenient service locations, flexible hours, and access to a range of in-house support services. Evaluations have shown significant decreases in sex work, needle sharing, and unregulated hormone injections, as well as increased condom use. Aksion Plus, founded in 1992, was the first youth NGO to address HIV through education and awareness-raising activities. The program now supports health and human rights interventions in six cities for young people who inject drugs, young sex workers, and young members of the LGBTQ community. Aksion Plus provides direct services and referrals for HIV and STI care, as well as opioid substitution therapy, including for young people in prisons and closed settings. Since 2000, outreach workers have also provided a needle and syringe program along with condom distribution. Through information, education, life skills, counseling, and capacity building, Aksion Plus aims to empower young key populations. The participation of young members of key populations as peer educators has been identified as essential to the success of interventions. Outreach workers play a critical role in linking the community to Aksion Plus while providing condoms, information materials, counseling, and referrals. The program also offers harm reduction training for other NGOs and government bodies, focusing on the needs of young people. The Boysproject is a social organization for male and transgender sex workers in and around Antwerp, Belgium. It uses social media to create demand for social and medical services and to provide information and referrals. The project hosts an online forum specifically for male and transgender sex workers, offering information and chat boxes for questions about sexual health and related issues. It also provides a drop-in center every Wednesday afternoon, advertised online and via SMS, where services and referrals are available from a social worker and a doctor. The drop-in center also offers a Dutch language course, a space for conversation, sharing experiences, and food. Boysproject collaborates with the Institute of Tropical Medicine to provide HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), which is not well-known among the sex worker community. Social workers play an important role in informing and accompanying individuals through the PEP process. In 2013, Boysproject services reached 298 sex workers, up from 229 in 2012. Around 1,130 invitations to the drop-in center were sent via social media in 2013, with 15–30 sex workers attending weekly. The PASMO/PSI Combination Prevention Program aims to increase access to HIV prevention interventions for key populations in six Central American countries. It seeks to reduce high-risk behaviors, decrease social hostility that fosters homophobia, stigma, and discrimination, increase access to essential prevention and health services, and strengthen strategic information through research and monitoring. A comprehensive package of interventions is provided for each target population, including behavioral, biomedical, and structural components. Services include participation in behavior change communication interventions, referrals for STI and opportunistic infection screening and treatment, medical care, and structural services such as family planning, stigma and discrimination support groups, legal support, and treatment for substance abuse. These services are delivered through close coordination with diverse partners, including Ministries of Health, donors, local NGOs, private laboratories, and clinics. AFEW (AIDS Foundation East-West) works in several countries to reduce the impact of HIV on key populations. Through client management initiatives, AFEW strengthens the capacities of local governmental, non-governmental, and community providers and supports the coordination of local service provider networks and resources. HIV client management is a collaborative process between the individual, the client manager, and local service providers, aimed at improving access to appropriate and timely health and psychosocial care. Client managers assist individuals in assessing their specific needs and developing strategies to address them effectively.
